strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: exploiting reward-free, mixed-quality offline experience to improve the online sample efficiency of visual reinforcement learning.

GSA is conceptually simple and coherent, combining world-model pre-training with retrieval-based rehearsal and a behavior-cloned guidance policy. The approach is potentially practical because trajectory retrieval can be implemented efficiently.

The experimental breadth is unusually strong: 72 pixel-based tasks spanning DMControl and Meta-World, with large improvements over Dreamer v3 and DrQ v2 at the same 150k-interaction budget and full per-task results for these comparisons.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes component ablations, compute estimates, hyperparameters, and comparisons covering representation learning, offline-data reuse, imitation learning, and world-model pre-training.
weaknesses: The central “non-curated data” premise is not convincingly supported. The Meta-World dataset is deliberately generated by task-specific TD-MPC2 agents on the same 50 tasks used downstream, including low-noise trajectories that may be near-expert demonstrations. Retrieval from a task's initial image can therefore recover same-task demonstrations. Dataset return and success distributions, held-out-task experiments, and held-out-embodiment experiments are needed to separate general transfer from reuse of task-specific behavior.

Broad superiority over methods using offline data is not established. Such baselines are evaluated on only six selected tasks rather than the full 72-task suite, while the aggregate comparison covers only training-from-scratch methods. The iVideoGPT numbers are imported from another paper with a different training setup, and parameter and compute parity is unclear given GSA's 280M-parameter model.

The claimed causal diagnosis of distribution shift is weak. It rests largely on one Shelf Place example, t-SNE plots, and a distance comparison for data explicitly selected by feature distance. The paper does not measure world-model prediction error or forgetting across distributions, relate these quantities to control performance, or compare against random retrieval in control experiments. The ER ablation also conflates rehearsal, rollout-state augmentation, and retrieval.

The theoretical appendix does not substantiate the method. Proposition 1 assumes retrieved states are closer—the desired conclusion—although the actual algorithm retrieves trajectories using initial-observation embeddings, and it incorrectly calls an expected Euclidean distance “total variation.” Proposition 2 merely asserts that an added loss prevents forgetting without proving a guarantee. Proposition 3 treats an alpha-coupling bound as an exact statewise policy mixture and does not model the algorithm's temporally contiguous policy switching.

Statistical and reporting quality is insufficient. Only three seeds are used; aggregate scores and full tables have no uncertainty or significance analysis; normalization and the calculation of the advertised 102.8% improvement are not defined. Moreover, Table 3 reports a Dreamer-v3-at-1M Meta-World mean of 0.900, whereas the 49 available per-task entries average approximately 0.656. One task also lacks all baseline results.

Important implementation details are absent, including the number of retrieved trajectories, BC update count, GSA's guidance start-time and duration distributions, Wasserstein-distance protocol, and evaluation-episode counts. No GSA code or dataset release is provided, and Algorithm 1 inconsistently writes rewards into batches from the stated reward-free dataset.

The continual-learning evidence is narrow and poorly matched: it uses one task sequence and only PackNet, grants access to all prior experience, and does not evaluate retention on earlier tasks. It therefore demonstrates forward adaptation more than continual-learning performance.

All experiments use in-domain simulators. Together with the same-task offline data and absence of held-out transfer, this substantially limits the claimed relevance to broadly available non-curated or in-the-wild data.

Algorithm 1 also assigns rewards to the nominally reward-free retrieval batch and ambiguously uses the duration variable as an ending timestep. Reproducing the main experiment reportedly requires roughly 1,728 GPU-hours.

The continual-adaptation experiment uses only one task sequence and PackNet as the sole baseline, and it reports current-task learning rather than retention on previous tasks. It therefore does not substantiate broader continual-learning claims.

The method is conceptually simple and coherent, combining world-model pretraining with retrieval-based rehearsal and behavior-cloned execution guidance.

The empirical scope is substantial: 72 pixel-control tasks, multiple seeds, full per-task results, and several component, sensitivity, and model-size ablations. The reported gains over learning from scratch are often large, especially on exploration-heavy tasks.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with readable figures and extensive appendices. weaknesses: The central “non-curated, task-agnostic” framing is questionable. Meta-World data are deliberately generated by reward-trained TD-MPC2 agents on the same 50 downstream tasks. Retrieval from one initial image achieves nearly perfect task-label precision, after which behavioral cloning can exploit successful exact-task trajectories. This resembles unlabeled target-task demonstrations more than naturally occurring task-agnostic data. There is no held-out-task/embodiment experiment or ablation excluding exact-task and successful trajectories.

The claimed distribution-shift diagnosis is not convincingly established. It relies primarily on one Shelf Place t-SNE visualization and an insufficiently specified Wasserstein analysis. No controlled experiment connects model prediction error or forgetting to the measured shift, while rehearsal simultaneously supplies favorable rollout initial states and execution guidance changes exploration. Thus the proposed mechanism is confounded with simpler access to task-relevant behavior.

The theoretical analysis does not support the implemented method. Proposition 1 assumes state-level epsilon-nearest retrieval, whereas the algorithm retrieves whole trajectories using a learned embedding of one initial observation; it also mislabels expected Euclidean distance as total variation and largely assumes its conclusion. The catastrophic-forgetting argument is only an assertion that an auxiliary loss regularizes. Proposition 2 analyzes a stationary action-level mixture, not the temporally contiguous scheduled policy switching used by NCRL, and requires a positive guide advantage that is never established for mixed-quality behavioral cloning.

The baseline evidence is incomplete and partly mismatched. The 72-task aggregate compares only against learning-from-scratch methods; offline-data methods are evaluated on six selected tasks. The headline iVideoGPT comparison uses different datasets, reward shaping, and demonstration initialization, while the aligned comparison covers only five endpoints. ExPLORe is materially modified after the authors fail to reproduce it. The 280M-parameter model and additional pretraining data/compute are aligned with DreamerV3 on only two tasks.

Statistical reporting is inadequate for the breadth of the claims: aggregate results lack uncertainty or significance tests, normalized-score construction is not defined, endpoint tables omit dispersion, and the manuscript inconsistently states three versus five NCRL seeds. Most component ablations cover only a few favorable tasks.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the appendix. No code or dataset release is identified, and important details such as the retrieval count, behavioral-cloning update count, switching distributions, loss coefficients, and update ratios are missing. The pseudocode also conflicts with the prose about whether H is a duration or endpoint and includes rewards in the nominally reward-free retrieved batch.

The continual-learning evidence is weak: NCRL is compared only with PackNet under asymmetric access to stored experience, and retention on previously learned tasks is not evaluated. More broadly, the algorithmic novelty is modest—largely DreamerV3 plus nearest-neighbor rehearsal and JSRL-like behavioral guidance—and the 280M model, 10M offline transitions, and substantial compute make “efficient” accurate only in terms of online environment interactions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: exploiting reward-free pooled experience to improve the sample efficiency of pixel-based online RL. The combination of world-model pretraining, retrieval-based rehearsal, and behavior-cloned execution guidance is coherent and practically motivated.

The empirical breadth is unusually strong: 72 tasks across Meta-World and DMControl, six embodiments, full per-task curves and tables, and substantial gains at 150k online steps. NCRL reaches 0.748 mean Meta-World success versus 0.430/0.360 for DrQ-v2/DreamerV3, and 617.7 mean DMControl return versus 226.5/320.9.

The study includes useful comparisons and ablations, including offline-data methods, an aligned iVideoGPT comparison, component ablations, retrieval corruption, guidance-schedule sensitivity, and a limited model-size control.

weaknesses: The central “non-curated” and task-agnostic framing is only partially supported. The Meta-World corpus is deliberately collected using TD-MPC-v2 agents on the same 50 downstream tasks; removing rewards and injecting noise still leaves task-specific demonstrations in the pool. Near-perfect retrieval precision reinforces that downstream tasks are directly covered. There is no held-out-task or held-out-embodiment evaluation, independently collected corpus, or real-world validation.

The claimed causal diagnosis of distribution shift is weakly established. It rests mainly on one Shelf Place visualization and a distance reduction largely induced by the retrieval rule itself. The paper does not measure world-model prediction error or forgetting broadly, and does not compare against random/full-data rehearsal or disentangle rehearsal, rollout-state augmentation, and guidance. The reported robustness even with 100% task-irrelevant retrieved data also weakens the argument that task-relevant retrieval is essential.

The broad 72-task evaluation compares only against learning-from-scratch methods. Offline-data competitors are evaluated on a small selected subset. NCRL uses a 280M-parameter model, while the matched-size DreamerV3 control covers only two tasks; thus model capacity and compute remain substantial confounds. The headline online-sample efficiency also excludes the 10M offline transitions and their collection cost.

The theoretical appendix is not sound as written. Proposition 1 assumes state-level epsilon-nearest retrieval although the algorithm retrieves whole trajectories using only initial-observation features, and it incorrectly calls expected Euclidean distance “total variation.” The catastrophic-forgetting argument is an assertion rather than a proof. Proposition 2 analyzes a per-state convex policy mixture that does not match the implemented temporally segmented switching policy, and its bound does not generally guarantee improvement.

Novelty is moderate: the main ingredients are established RSSM/Dreamer training, nearest-neighbor retrieval, rehearsal, behavior cloning, and JSRL-style policy switching. Reproducibility is also incomplete: there is no code or dataset release, the main text says three seeds whereas the appendix reports five for NCRL, aggregate tables lack uncertainty, and key details such as retrieval count, BC training budget, precise guidance-duration semantics, and dataset composition are missing or inconsistent. Overall, the strong results make the work promising, but these issues place it slightly below the acceptance threshold.
